summary: Proposes a set of technical services that each Internet mid-level (regional) network could offer inside its own network and to peer networks. It is informational and aims to help these networks provide consistent support.

eli5.summary: Regional networks were like middle-sized post offices. This paper suggests a list of helpful services each one should offer, so neighbors can work together smoothly.

subtitle: Technical services mid-level networks should offer to strengthen the Internet's hierarchy.

tldr.problem: The Internet has grown into a hierarchical structure of backbone, mid-level, and campus networks, but mid-level networks lack a standard set of services to offer their peer networks and connected sites, leading to inefficiency and inconsistency.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes that mid-level networks provide core technical services—DNS, network time, news distribution, mailing lists, software mirrors—and operational services like network information centers and coordinated problem resolution through network operations centers.
tldr.outcome: A structured approach to technical services makes mid-level networks more robust and enables them to support distributed applications and reduce unnecessary backbone traffic by serving content locally.

today: RFC 1291 is an Informational RFC proposing architectural services for mid-level networks. It has not been superseded, but reflects a moment in Internet history when the topology still relied on hierarchical mid-level regional networks. Since then, Internet topology has evolved with more direct interconnection and the rise of content delivery networks (CDNs), though the principles of distributed technical services remain relevant to modern network architecture.

sections.title: Growing Infrastructure and Decentralization
sections.content:
As the Internet expanded through the 1980s, it naturally organized itself into hierarchical layers: a national backbone (like NSFnet), mid-level networks serving geographic regions, and campus networks serving organizations. Each layer serves a different function and depends on services from the layer above it.

At the same time, the Internet's explosive growth made centralization impossible. Services like domain naming, whois lookup, and resource discovery are being decentralized so no single point fails. But this decentralization creates a challenge: mid-level networks lack a common set of services to offer each other and their end sites.
sections.eli5: The Internet was growing so fast it had to organize into layers—backbone, regional networks, and campus networks. Each layer needed to offer services to the ones below it, but no one had decided what those services should be.

sections.title: The Hierarchical Model
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a model where mid-level networks form a graph, interconnected to each other, each with multiple campus and organizational networks attached. This mirrors how organizational LANs work internally: they offer naming services, mail, shared files, and contact points for problems.

A mid-level network's services serve two roles: strengthening its own robustness (so regional network users are not dependent on backbone services for everything) and supporting end sites (campus networks) that connect to it. The model assumes mid-level networks are the highest functional division in the Internet's hierarchy at this point in time.
sections.eli5: The idea is to organize the Internet like an office building: the backbone is the main building, mid-level networks are floors, and campus networks are rooms. Each floor offers services so the rooms do not need to go all the way to the main building for every little thing.

sections.title: Core Technical Services
sections.content:
DNS traffic alone constituted 7% of NSFnet backbone traffic in May 1991. A mid-level network could dramatically reduce backbone load and improve reliability by hosting a nameserver that resolves queries for all directly attached domains, so name resolution works even if the mid-level network becomes isolated from the rest of the Internet.

Public domain software constitutes 23% of backbone traffic. Instead of every campus fetching from the same centralized archives (like uunet.uu.net), mid-level networks could offer cached software mirrors or pointers to resource discovery tools like Archie. Network Time Protocol (NTP) constituted 1% of traffic; mid-level networks should have at least one stratum-1 and two stratum-2 time servers so local sites do not overload global time sources.

Network News (Usenet) constitutes 14% of backbone traffic. A mid-level network can provide a news feed from one central hub instead of every campus connecting to an outside news site. Similarly, mailing lists could be served through mail exploders at the mid-level layer, reducing load on originating systems and simplifying administration.
sections.eli5: Five services make up the core: DNS so you can find computers by name, copies of popular software, time synchronization, news (Usenet), and mailing lists. Each of these was eating up a lot of backbone traffic that could be served locally instead.

sections.title: Operational and Information Services
sections.content:
Network Operations Centers (NOCs) at peer mid-level networks need to communicate to resolve problems. A mid-level NOC should maintain contact information for attached campus sites and peer networks, accessible via DNS TXT entries, finger, or a NOC phonebook. Coordinated NOC procedures enable rapid problem resolution when network links fail or sites lose connectivity.

Network Information Services (NIC) help end users discover resources—security advisories, library catalogs, password generators—and resolve problems. Mid-level networks can be the central point of contact for distributing this information hierarchically.

Experimental testbeds allow mid-level networks to cooperatively test and deploy new technologies (like White Pages directories or new routing schemas) before pushing them to production, with support and training for end sites.
sections.eli5: Beyond technical infrastructure, regional networks need ways to help each other solve problems (through NOCs), give users information (through NICs), and try out new technologies safely (through testbeds).

sections.title: A Structured Approach to Regional Networks
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that mid-level networks stop operating in isolation and instead adopt a standard set of technical and operational services. By hosting DNS, time, news, and software locally, they reduce backbone traffic and improve reliability. By coordinating through NOCs and operating experimental testbeds, they strengthen the entire Internet's ability to evolve.

This approach treats mid-level networks not as mere pass-through pipes but as active participants in Internet infrastructure, similar to how large organizations run their own IT services. The model acknowledges that the Internet is decentralized and works better when responsibility is distributed to local networks that understand their users' needs.
sections.eli5: Instead of all regions doing their own thing, if they offer the same services and work together, the whole Internet becomes stronger and faster.
